source.title: The activity-weight duality in feed forward neural networks: The geometric determinants of generalization
source.authors: Yu Feng; Wei Zhang; Yu-Hai Tu

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplemental information are present. The text identifies arXiv:2203.10736v3; the supplied title differs slightly from the paper title shown in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures generalization gaps and geometric properties across training recipes and regularization settings, using activity-weight duality rather than the measures in the listed claim versions. Its own results bear on V4, V5 and V6, and on measured properties related to V7, but it does not test the central random-label memorization/generalization claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports results varying SGD learning rate and batch size, weight decay and initialization, dropout fraction, training data size, mislabeled fraction, and decentralized versus synchronous SGD. The mislabeled-data results concern a fraction of randomly labeled examples, not a network trained entirely on random labels. Results cited from prior work, including large-model results in Zhang et al. [20], are not counted as rows. V1, V2, V3, V4, V5, V6, V7 and V8 are otherwise not directly tested as phrased; see version status and fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study investigates generalization using an activity-weight duality decomposition, but its own results do not directly test any listed version. Batch-size sweeps stop at a training-loss threshold rather than a fixed epoch budget; dropout sweeps report loss gaps rather than classification test error; and the geometric measures differ from V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors attribute generalization gaps to combined effective-gradient sharpness and dual-weight variation, and explain decentralized SGD's advantage through additional landscape-dependent noise and flatter solutions of similar size. Clarify that the CIFAR-10 accuracy numbers are attributed to prior study [20]; the present paper supplies their geometric analysis.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces and evaluates an activity-weight duality analysis of generalization gaps and compares SGD training settings and decentralized SGD; it is not a replication of the original studies underlying the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The generalization gap changes with learning rate, batch size, weight-decay rate, initialization scale, dropout fraction, training-set size, mislabeled fraction, and the SGD-based distributed algorithm.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing SGD learning rate decreases the loss gap, while increasing batch size increases it, principally through sharp-direction contributions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD hyperparameters affect generalization loss at a common low training-loss stopping threshold in this MNIST setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay reduces the loss gap and larger initialization increases it, predominantly through flat-direction contributions despite similar sharpness spectra.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective-gradient sharpness alone does not account for loss-gap differences when solution size varies.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss gap decreases at low dropout fractions and increases at high fractions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout has a non-monotonic effect on generalization loss in the tested MNIST network.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger training sets reduce the loss gap; partial random-label corruption increases it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data quantity and label corruption affect both geometric determinants and generalization loss.

fits_no_version.finding: At total batch size 1000, decentralized SGD yields 2.3% MNIST test error versus 2.6% for synchronous SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decentralized SGD can improve held-out classification performance relative to synchronous SGD at a common large batch size.

record.problems: The pair-wise gap is an approximation to the training/test gap, with training partner samples a subset of training data. The main text uses a small MNIST subset and a compact network for most parameter sweeps. Many conditions are reported qualitatively or in figures, without corresponding numerical values in the supplied text. Uncertainty is reported for the main learning-rate/batch-size sweeps but not for most other results. The CIFAR-10 large-model accuracy comparison is described as empirically demonstrated and uses only the reported algorithm comparison; uncertainty is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible result rows identified. Cited prior-study results and numerical results from the authors' earlier study [20] are excluded as prior work, not results from this study.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of entirely random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning scope, and the specified recovery strategies.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recovery of that performance difference through recipe adaptations.
Classification test-error comparisons with dropout, small-data exceptions, underfitting at excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures within a convolutional family.
Removal and retraining comparisons for highly memorized versus randomly selected examples.

record.verdict_notes: States marked cannot_determine concern the listed claim versions, not the validity of the reported standalone findings. The paper reports a correlation between its loss gap and test error in Fig. S4, but this does not provide dropout-specific classification-error comparisons. Its arguments against sharpness alone do not directly challenge V7's magnitude-aware measure.

versions.untested_parts: The paper varies a fraction of mislabeled training data, not training entirely on random labels, and does not compare random-label and natural-label held-out accuracy.
No network-width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks on the same image task; CIFAR-10 model comparisons in the paper are between distributed training algorithms.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers such as Adam with SGD on held-out performance.

The study varies batch size and reports generalization gaps, but does not test fixed-epoch, large-batch held-out performance or the specified adaptation recipes. It also compares decentralized and synchronous algorithms at a large total batch size.

Dropout fraction is varied and its generalization-gap effects are measured, but the study does not report the specified test-error comparison in fully connected and convolutional classifiers, small-training-set qualification, or combined dropout and weight-decay removal with augmentation.

The paper's dual-weight standard deviation and effective-gradient measures are not the magnitude-aware sharpness measure in V7, nor does it compare its ranking against the specified norm- and margin-based measures.
No memorized-example identification, removal, and retraining comparison.
